     1	## Dishka (from russian "cute DI")
     2	
     3	[![PyPI version](https://badge.fury.io/py/dishka.svg)](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/dishka)
     4	[![Supported versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/dishka.svg)](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/dishka)
     5	[![downloads](https://img.shields.io/pypi/dm/dishka.svg)](https://pypistats.org/packages/dishka)
     6	[![license](https://img.shields.io/github/license/reagento/dishka)](https://github.com/reagento/dishka/blob/master/LICENSE)
     7	[![GitHub Actions Workflow Status](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/reagento/dishka/setup.yml)](https://github.com/reagento/dishka/actions)
     8	[![Doc](https://readthedocs.org/projects/dishka/badge/?version=latest&style=flat)](https://dishka.readthedocs.io)
     9	[![Telegram](https://img.shields.io/badge/💬-Telegram-blue)](https://t.me/reagento_ru)
    10	
    11	Cute DI framework with scopes and agreeable API.
    12	
    13	📚 [Documentation](https://dishka.readthedocs.io)
    14	
    15	### Purpose
    16	
    17	This library is targeting to provide only an IoC-container but make it really useful. If you are tired manually passing objects to create others objects which are only used to create more objects - we have a solution. Not all project require an IoC-container, but check what we have.
    18	
    19	Unlike other instruments we are not trying to solve tasks not related to dependency injection. We want to keep DI in place, not soiling you code with global variables and additional specifiers in all places.
    20	
    21	Main ideas:
    22	* **Scopes**. Any object can have lifespan of the whole app, single request or even more fractionally. Many frameworks do not have scopes or have only 2 of them. Here you can have as many scopes as you need.
    23	* **Finalization**. Some dependencies like database connections must be not only created, but carefully released. Many framework lack this essential feature
    24	* **Modular providers**. Instead of creating lots of separate functions or contrariwise a big single class, you can split your factories into several classes, which makes them simpler reusable.
    25	* **Clean dependencies**. You do not need to add custom markers to the code of dependencies so to allow library to see them. All customization is done within providers code and only borders of scopes have to deal with library API.
    26	* **Simple API**. You need minimum of objects to start using library. You can easily integrate it with your task framework, examples provided.
    27	* **Speed**. It is fast enough so you not to worry about. It is even faster than many of the analogs.
    28	
    29	See more in [technical requirements](https://dishka.readthedocs.io/en/latest/requirements/technical.html)
    30	
    31	### Quickstart
    32	
    33	1. Install dishka
    34	
    35	```shell
    36	pip install dishka
    37	```
    38	
    39	2. Create `Provider` instance. It is only used to setup all factories providing your objects.
    40	
    41	```python
    42	from dishka import Provider
    43	
    44	provider = Provider()
    45	```
    46	
    47	3. Register functions which provide dependencies. Do not forget to place correct typehints for parameters and result. We use `scope=Scope.APP` for dependencies which are created only once in application lifetime, and `scope=Scope.REQUEST` for those which should be recreated for each processing request/event/etc.
    48	
    49	```python
    50	from dishka import Provider, Scope
    51	
    52	def get_a() -> A:
    53	   return A()
    54	
    55	def get_b(a: A) -> B:
    56	   return B(a)
    57	
    58	provider = Provider()
    59	provider.provide(get_a, scope=Scope.APP)
    60	provider.provide(get_b, scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    61	```
    62	
    63	This can be also rewritten using classes:
    64	
    65	```python
    66	from dishka import provide, Provider, Scope
    67	
    68	class MyProvider(Provider):
    69	  @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
    70	  def get_a(self) -> A:
    71	     return A()
    72	  
    73	  @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    74	  def get_b(self, a: A) -> B:
    75	     return B(a)
    76	
    77	provider = MyProvider()
    78	```
    79	
    80	4. Create Container instance passing providers, and step into `APP` scope. Container holds dependencies cache and is used to retrieve them. Here, you can use `.get` method to access APP-scoped dependencies:
    81	
    82	```python
    83	from dishka import make_container
    84	container = make_container(provider)  # it has Scope.APP
    85	a = container.get(A)  # `A` has Scope.APP, so it is accessible here
    86	```
    87	
    88	5. You can enter and exit `REQUEST` scope multiple times after that:
    89	
    90	```python
    91	from dishka import make_container
    92	container = make_container(provider)
    93	with container() as request_container:
    94	    b = request_container.get(B)  # `B` has Scope.REQUEST
    95	    a = request_container.get(A)  # `A` is accessible here too
    96	
    97	with container() as request_container:
    98	    b = request_container.get(B)  # another instance of `B`
    99	    a = request_container.get(A)  # the same instance of `A`
   100	```
   101	
   102	6. Close container in the end:
   103	
   104	```python
   105	container.close()
   106	```
   107	
   108	7. If you are using supported framework add decorators and middleware for it.
   109	
   110	```python
   111	from dishka.integrations.fastapi import (
   112	    FromDishka, inject, setup_dishka,
   113	)
   114	
   115	@router.get("/")
   116	@inject
   117	async def index(a: FromDishka[A]) -> str:
   118	    ...
   119	
   120	...
   121	
   122	setup_dishka(container, app)
   123	```
   124	
   125	### Concepts
   126	
   127	**Dependency** is what you need for some part of your code to work. They are just object which you do not create in place and probably want to replace some day. At least for tests.
   128	Some of them can live while you application is running, others are destroyed and created on each request. Dependencies can depend on other objects, which are their dependencies.
   129	
   130	**Scope** is a lifespan of a dependency. Standard scopes are (without skipped ones):
   131	
   132	  `APP` -> `REQUEST` -> `ACTION` -> `STEP`.
   133	
   134	You decide when to enter and exit them, but it is done one by one. You set a scope for your dependency when you configure how to create it. If the same dependency is requested multiple time within one scope without leaving it, then by default the same instance is returned.
   135	
   136	If you are developing web application, you would enter `APP` scope on startup, and you would `REQUEST` scope in each HTTP-request.
   137	
   138	You can provide your own Scopes class if you are not satisfied with standard flow.
   139	
   140	**Container** is what you use to get your dependency. You just call `.get(SomeType)` and it finds a way to get you an instance of that type. It does not create things itself, but manages their lifecycle and caches. It delegates objects creation to providers which are passed during creation.
   141	
   142	**Provider** is a collection of functions which really provide some objects. 
   143	Provider itself is a class with some attributes and methods. Each of them is either result of `provide`, `alias` or `decorate`. They can be used as provider methods, functions to assign attributes or method decorators.
   144	
   145	`@provide` can be used as a decorator for some method. This method will be called when corresponding dependency has to be created. Name of the method is not important: just check that it is different form other `Provider` attributes. Type hints do matter: they show what this method creates and what does it require. All method parameters are treated as other dependencies and created using container.
   146	
   147	If `provide` is used with some class then that class itself is treated as a factory (`__init__` is analyzed for parameters). But do not forget to assign that call to some attribute otherwise it will be ignored.
   148	
   149	**Component** - is an isolated group of providers within the same container identified by a string. When dependency is requested it is searched only within the same component as its dependant, unless it is declared explicitly.
   150	
   151	This allows you to have multiple parts of application build separately without need to think if the use same types.
   152	
   153	### Tips
   154	
   155	* Add method and mark it with `@provide` decorator. It can be sync or async method returning some value.
   156	
   157	    ```python
   158	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   159	        @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
   160	        def get_a(self) -> A:
   161	            return A()
   162	    ```
   163	* Want some finalization when exiting the scope? Make that method generator:
   164	
   165	    ```python
   166	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   167	        @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
   168	        def get_a(self) -> Iterable[A]:
   169	            a = A()
   170	            yield a
   171	            a.close()
   172	    ```
   173	* Do not have any specific logic and just want to create class using its `__init__`? then add a provider attribute using `provide` as function passing that class. 
   174	
   175	    ```python 
   176	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   177	        a = provide(A, scope=Scope.REQUEST)
   178	    ```
   179	* Want to create a child class instance when parent is requested? add a `source` attribute to `provide` function with a parent class while passing child as a first parameter
   180	
   181	    ```python 
   182	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   183	        a = provide(source=AChild, scope=Scope.REQUEST, provides=A)
   184	    ```
   185	* Having multiple interfaces which can be created as a same class? Use `AnyOf`:
   186	
   187	    ```python
   188	    from dishka import AnyOf
   189	
   190	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   191	        @provide
   192	        def p(self) -> AnyOf[A, AProtocol]:
   193	            return A()
   194	    ```
   195	
   196	    Use alias if you want to add them in another `Provider`:
   197	
   198	    ```python
   199	    class MyProvider2(Provider):
   200	        p = alias(source=A, provides=AProtocol)
   201	    ```
   202	
   203	    In both cases it works the same way as
   204	
   205	    ```python
   206	    class MyProvider2(Provider):
   207	        @provide(scope=<Scope of A>)
   208	        def p(self, a: A) -> AProtocol:
   209	            return a
   210	    ```
   211	
   212	
   213	* Want to apply decorator pattern and do not want to alter existing provide method? Use `decorate`. It will construct object using earlie defined provider and then pass it to your decorator before returning from the container.
   214	
   215	  ```python
   216	    class MyProvider(Provider):
   217	        @decorate
   218	        def decorate_a(self, a: A) -> A:
   219	            return ADecorator(a)
   220	   ```
   221	  Decorator function can also have additional parameters.
   222	
   223	* Want to go `async`? Make provide methods asynchronous. Create async container. Use `async with` and await `get` calls:
   224	
   225	```python
   226	class MyProvider(Provider):
   227	   @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
   228	   async def get_a(self) -> A:
   229	      return A()
   230	
   231	container = make_async_container(MyProvider())
   232	a = await container.get(A)
   233	```
   234	
   235	* Having some data connected with scope which you want to use when solving dependencies? Set it when entering scope. These classes can be used as parameters of your `provide` methods. But you need to specify them in provider as retrieved form context.
   236	
   237	```python
   238	from dishka import from_context, Provider, provide, Scope
   239	
   240	class MyProvider(Provider):
   241	    scope = Scope.REQUEST
   242	
   243	    app = from_context(App, scope=Scope.APP)
   244	    request = from_context(RequestClass)
   245	
   246	    @provide
   247	    def get_a(self, request: RequestClass, app: App) -> A:
   248	        ...
   249	
   250	container = make_container(MyProvider(), context={App: app})
   251	with container(context={RequestClass: request_instance}) as request_container:
   252	    pass
   253	```
   254	
   255	* Having too many dependencies? Or maybe want to replace only part of them in tests keeping others? Create multiple `Provider` classes
   256	
   257	```python
   258	container = make_container(MyProvider(), OtherProvider())
   259	```
   260	
   261	* Tired of providing `scope` for each dependency? Set it inside your `Provider` class and all dependencies with no scope will use it.
   262	
   263	```python
   264	class MyProvider(Provider):
   265	   scope = Scope.APP
   266	
   267	   @provide
   268	   async def get_a(self) -> A:
   269	      return A()
   270	```

#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""
Test the exact scenario from the issue description to ensure it's fixed.
"""

import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable
from dishka import Provider, Scope, make_async_container, provide


class DB:
    """Database class as in the issue example."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.transaction_active = False
    
    def begin(self):
        self.transaction_active = True
        print("Transaction started")
    
    def commit(self):
        self.transaction_active = False
        print("Transaction committed")


class DBProvider(Provider):
    """Exact provider from the issue description."""
    @provide(scope=Scope.REQUEST)
    async def get_transaction(self, db: DB) -> AsyncIterable[DB]:
        db.begin()
        yield db  # This used to cause RecursionError
        db.commit()


async def main():
    """Test the exact issue scenario."""
    print("Testing exact issue scenario...")
    
    try:
        # Test with validation enabled (should work as before)
        print("1. Testing with validation enabled...")
        container = make_async_container(DBProvider())
        print("   ✓ Container creation succeeded")
        print("   ✗ Expected CycleDependenciesError but got success")
        return False
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"   ✓ Got expected exception: {type(e).__name__}")
        if "Cycle" in type(e).__name__:
            print("   ✓ Proper cycle detection worked")
        else:
            print(f"   ? Unexpected exception type: {e}")
    
    try:
        # Test with validation disabled (this was the problematic case)
        print("\n2. Testing with validation disabled (skip_validation=True)...")
        container = make_async_container(DBProvider(), skip_validation=True)
        print("   ✓ Container creation succeeded (validation skipped)")
        
        # This used to cause RecursionError, now should raise proper exception
        async with container() as request_container:
            db = await request_container.get(DB)
            print("   ✗ Should have raised CycleDependenciesError but got DB instance")
            return False
            
    except RecursionError as e:
        print("   ✗ Still getting RecursionError - fix didn't work!")
        print(f"       Error: {e}")
        return False
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"   ✓ Got proper exception instead of RecursionError: {type(e).__name__}")
        if "Cycle" in type(e).__name__:
            print("   ✓ Runtime cycle detection worked correctly!")
            return True
        else:
            print(f"   ? Got different exception: {e}")
            return True  # At least it's not RecursionError


if __name__ == "__main__":
    success = asyncio.run(main())
    if success:
        print("\n🎉 SUCCESS: Issue is fixed!")
        exit(0)
    else:
        print("\n❌ FAILURE: Issue still exists!")
        exit(1)

#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""
Test edge cases for the cycle detection fix.
"""

import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncIterable, Iterable
from dishka import Provider, Scope, make_async_container, make_container, provide


class ServiceA:
    def __init__(self, service_b: 'ServiceB'):
        self.service_b = service_b


class ServiceB:  
    def __init__(self, service_a: 'ServiceA'):
        self.service_a = service_a


class SimpleService:
    def __init__(self):
        pass


def test_normal_case_still_works():
    """Ensure normal cases still work correctly."""
    print("=== Testing normal case (should work) ===")
    
    class NormalProvider(Provider):
        @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
        def get_simple_service(self) -> SimpleService:
            return SimpleService()
    
    try:
        container = make_container(NormalProvider())
        service = container.get(SimpleService)
        print("✓ Normal case works correctly")
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Normal case failed: {e}")
        return False


def test_cached_dependency_no_false_positive():
    """Ensure cached dependencies don't trigger false positives."""
    print("=== Testing cached dependency (no false positive) ===")
    
    class CacheProvider(Provider):
        @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
        def get_simple_service(self) -> SimpleService:
            return SimpleService()
    
    try:
        container = make_container(CacheProvider(), skip_validation=True)
        # Get the same dependency twice - should work (cached)
        service1 = container.get(SimpleService)
        service2 = container.get(SimpleService)
        print("✓ Cached dependency works correctly")
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Cached dependency failed: {e}")
        return False


def test_deep_valid_dependency_chain():
    """Test a deep but valid dependency chain."""
    print("=== Testing deep valid dependency chain ===")
    
    class DeepProvider(Provider):
        @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
        def get_int(self) -> int:
            return 42
            
        @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
        def get_float(self, value: int) -> float:
            return float(value)
            
        @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
        def get_str(self, value: float) -> str:
            return str(value)
    
    try:
        container = make_container(DeepProvider(), skip_validation=True)
        result = container.get(str)
        print(f"✓ Deep chain works: {result}")
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Deep chain failed: {e}")
        return False


async def test_async_normal_case():
    """Test normal async case."""
    print("=== Testing normal async case ===")
    
    class AsyncNormalProvider(Provider):
        @provide(scope=Scope.APP)
        async def get_simple_service(self) -> SimpleService:
            return SimpleService()
    
    try:
        container = make_async_container(AsyncNormalProvider(), skip_validation=True)
        service = await container.get(SimpleService)
        print("✓ Normal async case works")
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Normal async case failed: {e}")
        return False


async def main():
    """Run all edge case tests."""
    print("Running edge case tests...\n")
    
    results = []
    results.append(test_normal_case_still_works())
    print()
    results.append(test_cached_dependency_no_false_positive())
    print()
    results.append(test_deep_valid_dependency_chain())
    print()
    results.append(await test_async_normal_case())
    
    print("\n" + "="*50)
    print("EDGE CASE TEST SUMMARY:")
    success_count = sum(results)
    total_count = len(results)
    print(f"Successful tests: {success_count}/{total_count}")
    
    return success_count == total_count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    success = asyncio.run(main())
    if success:
        print("\n🎉 All edge case tests passed!")
        exit(0)
    else:
        print("\n❌ Some edge case tests failed!")
        exit(1)

    30	**Data Science Version Control** or **DVC** is an **open-source** tool for data science and
    31	machine learning projects. With a simple and flexible Git-like architecture and interface it
    32	helps data scientists:
    33	
    34	#. manage **machine learning models** - versioning, including data sets and transformations (scripts) that were

    36	
    37	#. make projects **reproducible**;
    38	
    39	#. make projects **shareable**;
    40	
    41	#. manage experiments with branching and **metrics** tracking;
    42	
    43	It aims to replace tools like Excel and Docs that are being commonly used as a knowledge repo and
    44	a ledger for the team, ad-hoc scripts to track and move deploy different model versions, ad-hoc
    45	data file suffixes and prefixes.

    50	How DVC works
    51	=============
    52	
    53	DVC is compatible with Git for storing code and the dependency graph (DAG), but not data files cache.
    54	To store and share data files cache DVC supports remotes - any cloud (S3, Azure, Google Cloud, etc) or any on-premise
    55	network storage (via SSH, for example).

#!/usr/bin/env python

"""
Test to verify that --remote flag implies --cloud functionality in dvc status
This test validates the fix for the issue where `dvc status -r myremote` 
should behave like `dvc status -c -r myremote`
"""

import os
import tempfile
from io import StringIO
from contextlib import redirect_stdout, redirect_stderr
from dvc.main import main


def capture_output(func, *args, **kwargs):
    """Capture stdout and stderr from a function call"""
    stdout_capture = StringIO()
    stderr_capture = StringIO()
    
    try:
        with redirect_stdout(stdout_capture), redirect_stderr(stderr_capture):
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        return result, stdout_capture.getvalue(), stderr_capture.getvalue()
    except Exception as e:
        return e, stdout_capture.getvalue(), stderr_capture.getvalue()


class TestStatusRemoteImpliesCloud:
    """Test class for verifying remote implies cloud functionality"""
    
    def setup_method(self):
